questions.question: Explain the terms monocotyledon and dicotyledon and describe how a soaked bean seed differs from a soaked mealie grain.
questions.expected_answer: Cotyledons are the seed leaves of the embryo. A monocotyledon has one cotyledon and a dicotyledon has two. A soaked bean (dicot) splits into two halves, each a large cotyledon storing food, with the small embryo between them. A soaked mealie grain (monocot) does not split; it has one small cotyledon pressed against a large starchy food store, the endosperm.

questions.question: Draw up a comparison of monocots and dicots under the headings leaves, roots, stems and flowers.
questions.expected_answer: Leaves: monocots usually long and narrow with parallel veins; dicots usually broad with branching, net-like veins. Roots: monocots have fibrous roots (many thin roots of similar size); dicots have a tap root (one main root with side branches). Stems: monocot vascular bundles are scattered; dicot vascular bundles are in a ring, so many dicots become woody and form growth rings. Flowers: monocot parts usually in threes or multiples of three; dicot parts usually in fours or fives.

questions.question: Classify the following as monocot or dicot, giving a reason for each: mealie, protea, aloe, bean, agapanthus.
questions.expected_answer: Mealie: monocot, one cotyledon, parallel-veined leaves, fibrous roots. Protea: dicot, net-veined leaves and a tap root, flower parts in fours. Aloe: monocot, parallel veins, fibrous roots, flower parts in multiples of three, despite thick leaves. Bean: dicot, two cotyledons, net-veined leaves, five petals, tap root. Agapanthus: monocot, flower parts in sixes, strap-like leaves with parallel veins.
